title: What actually updates the handbook?
text: Someone at company asks when they should update the employee handbook. The wrong first answer is a date on the calendar. Liam is here to take them through the real trigger.

title: The yearly review leaves a gap
text: The obvious plan is a yearly review. Read the whole handbook every December. Fix what looks stale. But a law that changes in March doesn't wait for December. The section it touches is wrong the day the law takes effect and it stays wrong for however many months are left until the scheduled read through. The fix isn't reviewing more

title: One law change, one section
text: Often. It's tracking updates by what actually triggers them, a specific legal change. Watch the anchor. A state raises its paid leave minimum in the spring. That one change touches exactly one section, the leave policy, not the whole handbook. That section gets a specific

title: Logged, not finished
text: Fix, new language for the new minimum logged with what changed, why, and the date it took effect. So there's a record instead of a silent override. But a flagged section isn't a finished one. The drafted language still needs a legal read before it ships. And a quiet quarter with no flags doesn't mean the handbook is complete. It means no tracked law changed, which isn't the same thing. title: Your turn
text: Prompt. Read it with me. Pick one policy in your employee handbook, leave, overtime, remote work, anything. Write down the date it was last actually changed and find out whether any law touching that topic has changed since.
